questions.prompt: What does rms mean for a sinusoidal AC voltage?
questions.answer: RMS means root-mean-square. For a sinusoidal voltage, it is the equivalent DC voltage that would produce the same average heating in a resistor.

questions.prompt: State the relationship between angular frequency \(\omega\) and frequency \(f\).
A sinusoidal voltage has peak value \(170\,\mathrm V\). Find its rms value.
An AC signal has frequency \(60\,\mathrm{Hz}\). Find its angular frequency.
A sinusoidal current has \(I_{\mathrm{rms}}=3.0\,\mathrm A\). Find its peak current.
questions.answer:
For a sinusoid,
\[
I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{I_0}{\sqrt2}
\]
so
\[
I_0=\sqrt2I_{\mathrm{rms}}=4.24\,\mathrm A
\]

questions.prompt: A voltage is \(v(t)=80\cos(100\pi t)\,\mathrm V\). Find the peak voltage, rms voltage, angular frequency, frequency, and period.
questions.answer:
The peak voltage is
\[
V_0=80\,\mathrm V
\]
The rms voltage is
\[
V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{80}{\sqrt2}=56.6\,\mathrm V
\]
The angular frequency is
\[
\omega=100\pi\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}
\]
so
\[
f=\frac{\omega}{2\pi}=50\,\mathrm{Hz}
\]
and
\[
T=\frac{1}{f}=0.020\,\mathrm s
\]

questions.prompt: Voltage is \(v(t)=V_0\cos(\omega t+30^\circ)\) and current is \(i(t)=I_0\cos(\omega t-10^\circ)\). What is the phase difference, and which signal leads?
questions.answer:
The phase difference of voltage relative to current is
\[
\phi=30^\circ-(-10^\circ)=40^\circ
\]
The voltage has the larger phase angle, so voltage leads current by \(40^\circ\).

questions.prompt: A sinusoidal voltage is \(120\,\mathrm V\) rms at \(50\,\mathrm{Hz}\) with zero phase. Write \(v(t)\) using cosine form.
questions.answer:
First find the peak voltage:
\[
V_0=\sqrt2V_{\mathrm{rms}}=120\sqrt2=170\,\mathrm V
\]
The angular frequency is
\[
\omega=2\pi(50)=100\pi\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}
\]
Thus
\[
v(t)=170\cos(100\pi t)\,\mathrm V
\]

questions.prompt: Show that the rms value of \(V_0\cos\omega t\) is \(V_0/\sqrt2\).
questions.answer:
The rms value is defined by
\[
V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\langle v^2\rangle}
\]
For \(v=V_0\cos\omega t\),
\[
\langle v^2\rangle=V_0^2\langle\cos^2\omega t\rangle
\]
Over a full cycle,
\[
\langle\cos^2\omega t\rangle=\frac12
\]
so
\[
V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{V_0^2}{2}}=\frac{V_0}{\sqrt2}
\]

questions.prompt: Two sinusoidal voltages of the same frequency have rms values \(30\,\mathrm V\) and \(40\,\mathrm V\), with a \(90^\circ\) phase difference. Find the rms value of their phasor sum.
questions.answer:
For phasors at right angles, add by Pythagoras:
\[
V_{\mathrm{rms,net}}=\sqrt{30^2+40^2}=50\,\mathrm V
\]
The result uses rms values because phasor magnitudes can be consistently represented by rms magnitudes.
